title: Organised crime inside the state
summary:
Drug traffickers, mafias, smuggling rings and gangs get their own people inside the institutions meant to stop them, in 96 countries on this map and from the 1950s to this year. What they want is much the same everywhere: no arrest, no extradition, warning before a raid, safe passage for their goods. Where a route runs through a port or a border post, they buy the officials in the way, often not one or two but most of a shift: Romanian prosecutors indicted dozens of officers at one crossing, and Laos disciplined 78 for letting people through unrecorded.

Along the cocaine routes, from the Andes through Central America and Mexico to the US border, traffickers have bought police chiefs, generals, governors and judges, and in parts of Mexico whole town police forces have worked for a cartel. The trade crosses the Atlantic through small West African states into the container ports of Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain, where networks recruit dock workers and customs staff. In northern Europe officers sell case files, and detectives in Chile and the Bahamas sold warrants and patrol-boat positions.

The newer cases reach further into the parts of the state that decide guilt. Judges in Kuwait were jailed for taking a laundering suspect's gifts, prosecutors in Bulgaria and Costa Rica are accused of working for criminal groups from inside the office that decides who is charged, and the United States sanctioned Liberia's chief prosecutor over bribes to drop cases. Bulgaria's largest gambling operator is alleged to have had inside his criminal group the inspection chief who policed him.

In other places the criminal, or a politician working for him, holds office, in parliaments from India to Brazil. Italy has dissolved town councils and health authorities 402 times since 1991 because a mafia group had taken hold of them, and prosecutors there describe the bargain as votes for access: the clan delivers the votes that elect a mayor and then has a say over the town hall it helped fill. In Colombia roughly 30% of Congress was investigated or convicted over collusion with cocaine-exporting paramilitary armies.

For people who live with this, reporting a trafficker can mean reporting to someone the trafficker pays, and a judge may have been paid before the case is heard.
uncertain: Much of this record comes from trials abroad, and an official charged in another country can stay in office at home. Several cases rest on US indictments, sanctions or trial testimony that no court has tested against the person named. A large share of the newer entries sit at the charge stage: prosecutors' allegations against border officers, police commanders, prosecutors, judges and mayors that have not been tried, and in Mexico the officials suspected of taking traffickers' money while running the national Interpol office were later acquitted. One claim, that scam operators paid Myanmar's home affairs minister, comes from a single report that gives no evidence, and the rest of what is alleged about scam-compound builders there comes from sanctions and press investigations rather than court findings.

title: China's long arm abroad
summary:
China's Communist Party runs a department, the United Front Work Department, whose job is to win friends and influence among Chinese communities, business people and politicians abroad. Alongside it, China's main spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, and military intelligence recruit people close to power. Courts, security services and parliamentary inquiries in at least ten countries, from the Pacific islands and Taiwan to North America and Europe, have found them reaching into parties, election campaigns, ministers' offices, parliaments, city halls and defence and research work.

Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own, is a main target. Chinese officials pay for village chiefs' trips to the mainland and use them to urge the chiefs to vote for a chosen party, and Beijing recruits retired admirals, former cabinet officials, soldiers and aides near the president.

In Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Britain and the United States, the usual route is a well-connected donor or community leader who chairs a United Front-linked group, gives to parties and gets close to MPs, in some cases paying an MP's bills or placing a relative or intern in an MP's office. In 2026 the mayor of a Californian city pleaded guilty to acting as a Chinese agent. In Europe, the people working for Chinese intelligence or Party bodies have included an MEP's aide, a researcher in the UK Parliament and a Huawei executive in Poland, and in North America others have worked inside defence contractors, government laboratories and the State Department, passing technology and documents to China.

In the Pacific islands the money goes straight to lawmakers: Solomon Islands MPs said China and Taiwan each offered them large sums to sway parliament's choice of which to recognise. Inside UN agencies, Chinese nationals in senior posts have been accused of using them for Beijing; a former head of the UN's economic department said on Chinese television that he had a Uyghur leader removed from a UN forum.

For voters, this means some candidates on the ballot, from parliament down to the city council, were chosen, paid for or run on Beijing's instructions without voters being told, and some MPs vote after taking money that started in China. Many cases end without a conviction, because the money passes through middlemen and intelligence reports seldom name names.
uncertain: The former UN official's account of having a Uyghur leader removed from a UN forum is his own statement on Chinese television. Accusations that other Chinese nationals in senior UN posts served Beijing come from critics and governments, not from any finding by the UN. Several of the European and North American cases are charges or security-service findings that have not been tested in court. The Solomon Islands account is the MPs' own statement, not a court finding.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
Russia reaches into other countries' politics by two routes, and which one it uses depends on how strong the state it is dealing with is. Where a government is weak and fighting rebels, as in parts of Africa, Russia places its own people inside the state itself. Where a government is strong and elected, as across the European Union and its neighbours, it works through individual politicians, paying them or running them as sources, so that a speech, a vote or a party's line serves Moscow while appearing to be the politician's own.

In Africa the main vehicle was the Wagner Group, a private military company run by the businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin, whose strategists paid candidates in Madagascar's presidential election. In the Central African Republic the placement goes well beyond advice. A Wagner-linked Russian became the president's national security adviser in 2018, and by 2023 UN reporting and investigative groups described Russian intelligence officers in the presidency's security circle, a Russian running the police partnership, Wagner officers commanding units of the national army, and Wagner's proxies holding posts in the cabinet. Its companies were granted state mining permits by decree, and the group The Sentry says Wagner also worked on the mining law that would govern them, so one foreign party held the permits, the posts and a hand in the rules.

In Europe the money tends to travel through go-betweens rather than straight from the Russian state. The clearest example is Voice of Europe, a site run from Prague that passed Russian money to politicians in several EU countries until Czech intelligence exposed it in 2024. Members of the European Parliament from Britain, Germany, Latvia and Hungary appear in these cases as having taken Russian money or reported to Russian intelligence. In Ukraine a close ally of Vladimir Putin led the main opposition party, and in Moldova Russia funded a whole party and a court jailed one of its elected governors.

For people living in these countries, it means a politician they voted for may be speaking for a foreign government without their knowing, and in the Central African Republic that who the army fights, who guards the president and who gets a mining permit are settled partly by men working for another state.
uncertain: Several cases rest on sanctions, intelligence briefings, leaked emails or recordings, or press reporting rather than court rulings. The German and Latvian MEPs have not been convicted, and the Ukrainian opposition leader's treason charge rests on the Ukrainian government's case. The Central African Republic now carries much of this pattern's weight, and the account of Wagner's cabinet posts, army commands and hand in the mining law there comes from UN reporting and investigative groups, with no court having tested it.

summary:
Governments reach into other countries by paying, or planting, people who hold office there: legislators, diplomats, ministers' aides, members of the European Parliament, UN officials and staff at technology companies. The cases run from the 1970s to today, and the sponsors range from neighbours to distant powers, among them Russia, India, Iran, Egypt, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Morocco, Hungary, Cuba, South Korea, and earlier Saddam Hussein's Iraq and Muammar Gaddafi's Libya. The money usually passes through a businessman, a lobbyist or a company the foreign state controls, so that on paper it looks like a gift, a consulting fee, free travel or a campaign donation.

The targets are not only national governments. Saddam's Iraq gave oil allocations to the head of the UN's Oil-for-Food programme, North Korea chose the local staff of a UN agency and kept their pay, and Hungarian intelligence officers at Hungary's EU mission tried to recruit European Commission staff.

Most documented cases are in the United States, Canada and Brussels, because prosecutors and oversight bodies there publish what they find; 10 of the 25 cases in this pattern are American. In 2024 a New York jury convicted Senator Bob Menendez, who chaired the committee that shapes US arms sales, of acting as Egypt's agent for cash and gold bars. Spy services place their own people inside the state for decades; Cuba's intelligence service had an officer in the US diplomatic service for more than 40 years, rising to ambassador. At the far end, one government takes over another's offices outright: UN experts report that Rwanda's army commands the M23 armed group in eastern Congo and has put Rwandans in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control in the areas it holds.

For the people living there, the result is officials who answer to someone they did not elect. Votes in a parliament or an international body, an arms decision or a provincial tax office can be bought for another country's benefit. Many cases stop short of a verdict. Canada's parliamentary intelligence committee found that some MPs and senators knowingly took part in foreign interference but named none of them, and several US cases ended in acquittal, dismissal or a pardon, leaving voters without a settled account.
uncertain: Rwanda's command of M23 rests on UN expert reports, not a court verdict, and Rwanda denies it. India rejects the Canadian findings. The Oil-for-Food payment to the programme's head is the finding of an independent inquiry, not a conviction.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary:
Governments that want a softer report on their human-rights record, a vote on trade or a friendly speech pay members of Europe's parliaments to deliver it. The targets are the European Parliament in Brussels, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, where MPs from 46 countries judge elections and human rights, and national parliaments whose members also sit in those bodies. The payers in the cases on this map are Azerbaijan, Qatar, Morocco and Russia, along with Chinese state interests and the Chinese telecoms company Huawei, and the same methods have now reached the circle around Israel's prime minister.

The money rarely arrives as a plain bribe. It comes as consultancy fees routed through shell companies, as cash passed through a human-rights charity, as paid advertising in an MP's newspaper, as gifts, travel and football tickets, or as payments from a go-between in a third country, sometimes a former MP. Russia's money has come through a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician and a Prague news site he ran. Alongside the money, Russian and Chinese intelligence have placed or recruited people inside the European Parliament, from MEPs to assistants. Most of it came out through leaked bank records, police raids and seized cash.

Azerbaijan's network is the widest. The Azerbaijani Laundromat moved $2.9 billion through shell companies, some of it to European politicians, and an inquiry found in 2018 that Azerbaijani money had reached Assembly members from at least six countries; one of them, an Italian group leader later jailed for it, helped defeat a report on the people Azerbaijan jails for their politics. In 2022 Belgian police found bags of cash at the home of a European Parliament vice-president in a case prosecutors say was paid for by Qatar and Morocco. Courts in Italy, Germany, Hungary and Britain have now convicted current or former members.

For voters, this means the person they elected may be speaking and voting for another government on human rights, trade or security, and they cannot see it until police find the money. The people most directly harmed are those the reports were meant to protect: prisoners, opposition figures and journalists in the paying countries. Cases take years, and accused members keep their seats while parliament decides whether to lift the immunity that protects them from prosecution.
uncertain: The Qatar and Morocco case in Brussels, the Huawei case and the Israeli case are investigations or charges, not convictions; Belgian prosecutors later said one MEP named in the Huawei case was a different man with the same name.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Since the failed military coup of July 2016, Turkey's government has treated the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen that ran schools and businesses in many countries, as an enemy that had hidden itself inside the state. It says Gülen followers spent decades taking posts in the police, courts and army, calls the movement a terrorist group, 'FETÖ', and blames it for the coup. The movement denies organising the coup, though Turkish courts have convicted hundreds of officers for it.

Part of how followers got in is on the record. The questions for Turkey's 2010 civil-service entrance exam were leaked in advance, which helped place Gülen followers in state jobs, and in the same year candidates linked to the movement won control of the board that appoints and promotes judges and prosecutors. Prosecutors and gendarmes tied to the movement later turned those posts against the government, summoning the head of the national intelligence agency for questioning and stopping its lorries.

Inside Turkey, the response has been removal by decree rather than by trial. About 150,000 people lost public jobs after the coup without a court ruling on each person, among them judges, police officers, soldiers and teachers. The clearest single instance came the day after the coup, when about a third of Turkey's judges were removed at once. The label has since reached a deputy head of the Constitutional Court and a judge at a UN war-crimes tribunal.

The Gülen movement is not the first group to get inside the Turkish state. In the 1970s the leader of the Grey Wolves, the militant youth wing of a nationalist party, served as deputy prime minister, and in 1996 a car crash at Susurluk showed a wanted Grey Wolves gunman travelling with a senior police officer and a member of parliament. Turkey's own reach abroad is on the record too: in 2018 Kosovo's police and intelligence service seized six Turks and handed them to Ankara, behind the back of Kosovo's own prime minister.

For Turks, it has meant a justice system where a prosecutor's or judge's first loyalty could lie with a movement, followed by one where being named as a Gülen follower can cost a teacher, judge or police officer their job with no individual hearing.
uncertain: Turkish courts accepted that the Gülen movement organised the 2016 coup, but the movement denies it. The movement's role in the 2010 judicial board election rests largely on later Turkish government and court accounts, and the convictions of the Constitutional Court deputy head and the UN tribunal judge are disputed.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary:
Religious movements and church-linked lobbies get their members into ministries, parliaments, courts and police forces in 13 countries on this map, from Japan and South Korea through India and Turkey to Brazil and the United States. Most do it openly. A movement trains politicians or builds a parliamentary league or party of its own, and its members vote together on schools, family law and the constitution. Others supply what campaigns need: volunteers, donations, a congregation's votes, or mass sign-ups before candidates are chosen.

In some countries one movement shapes most of the government. In India the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, trains many of the people who run the governing BJP; a press count found 38 of the 53 ministers in Narendra Modi's second government had RSS roots. In Japan, 10 of the 19 ministers in the cabinet formed in 2025 belong to the parliamentary league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby. Evangelical churches hold a bloc of more than 200 of the 513 seats in Brazil's lower house.

Money is the main tool of the movements with the widest reach. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, has given cash and luxury gifts to South Korean politicians and the president's wife, and signed thousands of followers up to the ruling party before its leadership vote; in 2026 its leader was jailed there for bribing politicians. In Japan it worked on staffing too, circulating notices to recruit younger believers into jobs as lawmakers' secretaries, while its own publications cast a senior figure in the governing party as its standing channel to the leadership.

A few movements have placed members in secret. In the 1970s the Church of Scientology planted a clerk inside the US tax authority to copy its files. Turkey says the Gülen movement, a religious network, spent decades placing followers as police, judges and officers; after the failed 2016 coup it dismissed about 150,000 public employees by decree, without a court ruling on each person.

Where many ministers share one movement's training, people outside it find laws on religion and schooling written without them. Where a church buys access, its donations become political money, primaries can be decided by congregations signed up in bulk, and a lawmaker's staff may owe the movement their job.
uncertain: Membership of a lawful religious group or lobby is not wrongdoing, and several membership counts, including the RSS and Nippon Kaigi figures, come from press reports and league lists, not official records. Turkey's account of Gülen placements rests largely on government decrees, not individual court findings. The Japanese material on the Unification Church comes from the church's own notices and publications and from press reporting: in one entry an education ministry reversed an 18-year refusal to let the church change its name after a church-linked editor bought tickets to the minister's fundraisers, and no source connects the two.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary:
In parts of South and East Asia, movements that want the state to defend one religion, or one national identity tied to a religion, have their members in cabinet, in parliament, on law-drafting panels and on public boards.

In India and Japan the route is through the governing party. In India, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, is the body from which the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) grew. It lends the party organisers and supplies much of its leadership: Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser, and a 2020 count by the news site ThePrint found that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers had RSS roots. The RSS also sends one of its own organisers to hold the BJP's top organisational post, and the leader of its history wing was made head of the national history research council. In Japan, a nationalist lobby, Nippon Kaigi, and the political arm of the Shinto shrine association each keep a league of members of parliament that backs constitutional revision and official honours for the Yasukuni Shrine, where Japan's war dead, including convicted war criminals, are enshrined. Press counts put 15 of the 19 ministers in Shinzo Abe's 2014 cabinet in Nippon Kaigi's league, and 10 of 19 in the cabinet Sanae Takaichi, herself a league member, formed in 2025.

In Buddhist-majority Myanmar and Sri Lanka, monks' movements have been given a direct hand in writing the law. In Myanmar, texts proposed by Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group, became four laws in 2015 that regulate religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and men of other faiths. In Sri Lanka, a president put the leader of an anti-Muslim monks' group in charge of drafting a single legal code.

In Bangladesh and Pakistan the route is covert. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that campaigns for one Islamic state across Muslim countries, has recruited serving army officers, including a Pakistani brigadier, and in Bangladesh officers linked to it were accused of plotting a coup in 2012.

For religious minorities, this means living under laws and officials shaped by groups that favour the majority faith, in matters as close to home as whom they may marry and whether they may change religion.
uncertain: The Japanese counts come from a Communist Party newspaper and press reports of league lists, not from official records. The RSS does not publish membership rolls, so counts of ministers with RSS roots are journalists' estimates.

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
Governments hire consulting, accounting and lobbying firms to redesign agencies and draft laws, and the same firms sell advice to the companies those laws cover. Most of this is lawful. The cases here are where the arrangement let a firm, or the company paying it, steer the state from inside. They come mostly from Britain, Australia and France, where these firms do much government work, and from Africa, where Western firms dealt with state companies.

The commonest route is people moving between the firm and the ministry. Partners and staff are lent to a treasury or a cabinet office to help write rules, then return to advise clients on the same rules; in Australia a partner from one of these firms, advising the Treasury on tax-avoidance law, shared its confidential plans with dozens of his firm's colleagues. A second route is a financier given a desk at the centre of government, as Greensill Capital's founder was in Downing Street, while the government's former chief commercial officer advised the firm. A third is a company getting a minister to work for it from inside the government, as leaked files show France's economy minister did for Uber.

At the far end, a consultancy can help capture a whole institution. In South Africa a judicial inquiry found that Bain & Company, a US consultancy, helped President Jacob Zuma's allies take control of the national tax service, and its restructuring cut the unit that produced a third of the service's revenue. In the same years foreign consultancies paid officials at South Africa's state power and rail companies to win contracts. The body reached into need not be a ministry: a Canadian engineering group paid officials in Gaddafi-era Libya, and at home paid $22.5 million to the chief executive and a senior manager of a Montreal teaching hospital, who then shaped the tender so that the firm won the building contract.

For taxpayers, it means a law can be shaped by advisers whose paying clients gain from its gaps, and the shortfall falls on everyone else. Because consulting reports are usually unpublished, voters cannot see who shaped a policy. Most of this came out through public inquiries, leaked files and court cases, not through routine disclosure.
uncertain: Bain denies that it knowingly helped take over South Africa's tax service. The French Uber case rests on leaked company files (the 'Uber Files').

title: Global firms buying governments
summary:
Large companies win public contracts and favourable laws by paying the officials who decide them, and this map records it in 19 countries. The pattern is strongest wherever the state owns the valuable asset: oil and mining, state investment funds, road and port contracts and power utilities. The payers are construction groups, commodity traders, shipbuilders, banks and utilities, and the money moves through intermediaries, shell companies or a department set up for the purpose, so the bribe appears as a consulting fee or a campaign donation.

The largest case is Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group that admitted to US authorities in 2016 that it paid $788 million in bribes across Latin America and Africa; its money reached presidents, vice-presidents and campaigns from Mexico to Angola, and when Ecuador's state auditor fined its projects, the firm paid the comptroller general more than $10 million and the fines were cancelled. Swiss-based commodity traders have admitted bribing officials at state oil companies in Nigeria, Congo and Angola. State borrowing is another route: in Malaysia and Mozambique, bankers and a shipbuilder paid officials while arranging loans and bonds that left the public with the debt.

In a few places a business reached the cabinet itself. In South Africa a judicial inquiry found that ministers and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma who offered ministries to officials willing to cooperate. In the United States, power companies have paid state lawmakers to pass laws in their favour.

Alongside the bribes runs a legal route in the United States. A former co-chairman of the investment bank Goldman Sachs, as Treasury Secretary, argued for repealing a banking law the industry wanted gone; its former chief ran the AIG rescue that paid Goldman $12.9 billion in full; and a former Goldman economist led the New York Federal Reserve, whose supervisors were recorded deferring to the bank.

Most of what is known came out through US and Swiss prosecutions, because those countries can charge foreign companies that use their banks. Bribes are added to the price of roads, power and oil deals, countries lose revenue on resources sold cheaply, and in Peru and Ecuador the courts found that the leaders who awarded the contracts were the ones who were paid.
uncertain: No court has found the moves of Goldman Sachs staff into government illegal.

title: Industries inside their regulators
summary:
Companies get inside the bodies that regulate them, buy from them or write their industry's rules. They do it in four ways: paying officials, putting their own people in official posts, handing regulators and lawmakers text adopted as the official version, and buying the inspector or auditor meant to check them. The record now covers 67 countries.

Paying officials is the best documented, because companies often settle with US, British, Swiss or Norwegian prosecutors. Builders, commodity traders, arms dealers, loggers, drug and software firms from the United States, Europe, China and Brazil have paid, or been charged with paying, the officials who award contracts at state oil and power companies, defence ministries, state banks and public hospitals on four continents. The largest case is the Brazilian builder Odebrecht, which admitted paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries.

The second is the firm's own people in the official seat. In Washington the environment, energy, food, securities and telecoms regulators have been run by former lobbyists or executives from the industries they oversee, who then weakened rules those industries opposed. In Niger an arms dealer's company was given the defence ministry's own signing power, so it could approve its own deals.

The third is getting inside the rule-making. Regulators of nuclear power, aircraft, medicines, food and pesticides in the United States, Japan and Europe have let the industries they oversee check their own products, or draft passages of official reviews, and US state legislatures have copied thousands of industry-written bills. It happens contract by contract too: a supplier's staff wrote tender specifications with Chinese hospital directors so that only its own equipment qualified.

The fourth, which the newer cases add most to, is the checking itself. Odebrecht paid Ecuador's comptroller general more than $10 million and the fines on its projects were cancelled, and a firm in Italy is accused of paying serving police to search state databases for its clients. Officials of international bodies go the same way, from aid and UN procurement to football federations whose presidents admitted taking marketing firms' money. The cost shows up in safety and in public budgets: Boeing employees still do much of the safety certification of Boeing planes, which a congressional committee found weakened oversight before two crashes killed 346 people.
uncertain: Some cases rest on reporting, not on findings: the logging payments in Congo and Gabon come from investigators' and reporters' accounts. A good share of the newer entries are allegations that prosecutors have brought but no court has yet tried, in Congo-Brazzaville, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, Italy and the United States, so the pattern now leans more on untested material than it did. The US appointments from industry were lawful and made in public; the link to a former employer is read from what the official's later decisions did, not from proof that anyone gave instructions.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, through their foreign branch the Quds Force, arm and fund Shia militias and parties across the Middle East, and in some countries those groups have moved inside the state. They are written into the armed forces by law, they hold seats in parliament and the cabinet, their commanders run interior ministries, their men sit over defence purchasing and tax collection, or their partners hold state monopolies. Iran gets fighters that another country's budget pays for, and a say in its decisions.

Iraq is the clearest case. Since 2005 commanders of the Badr Organization, a militia founded in Iran, have run the Interior Ministry, which controls the police. Since a 2016 law the Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of about 67 armed groups almost all backed by the Guards, have been a branch of Iraq's armed forces paid from the state budget, and in 2024 their chief of staff said publicly that they took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Some brigades on that payroll are run by groups the United States lists as terrorist organisations, and in 2026 Iran-aligned groups placed their own nominees as ministers while keeping their armed wings.

Yemen shows a second shape, where the armed movement is itself the authority. UN investigators say the man buying weapons for the defence ministry in Sanaa is attached to an office in Tehran, that a Quds Force general stands over the Houthi military commands, and that a Hezbollah-linked expert is alleged to guide the committee that sets customs duties, taxes and telephone tariffs and plans military spending.

The network also reaches through money. In West Africa and South America, the US Treasury says people tied to Hezbollah, a Lebanese Shia party with its own armed wing aligned with Iran, got close to presidents through business deals or bribes; in Gambia they received the fuel supply monopoly and half the state telecoms companies.

For people in these countries, taxes pay for armed units that answer to another country's leader, and a cabinet cannot settle questions of war and peace by itself, because some parties at the table keep their own armies. Where Hezbollah's backers held monopolies, people paid for fuel and phone calls through companies whose profits, by one journalists' estimate, sent more than $100 million to Hezbollah.
uncertain: The figure of more than $100 million reaching Hezbollah through these monopolies is one journalists' estimate. Much of the evidence outside the Middle East, including the claims about Paraguay's leaders, is US sanctions, not court verdicts. The Yemen entries come from a UN panel of experts reporting what its investigators and sources say, and the Hezbollah-linked adviser's role on the revenue committee is given there as an allegation; none of it has been tested in court.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
Private clubs, think tanks and legal networks bring officials together with business leaders and like-minded allies, away from the public record. Belonging to them is lawful. The cases kept here are those where the private body did more than host meetings: it wrote the papers, bills or lists of appointees that government then used as its own. All of them are in the United States, and they run from 1939 to today.

The methods differ. During the Second World War the Council on Foreign Relations, a private foreign-policy club paid for by the Rockefeller Foundation, secretly wrote the State Department's postwar planning papers, which the department classified and circulated as its own; one of its study-group leaders, Allen Dulles, was recruited by the wartime spy agency to carry out its plans for occupied Germany. Think tanks write a programme for an incoming government and supply the people to run it: the Reagan administration acted on about 60% of the 2,000 proposals in the Heritage Foundation's 1981 plan for it, and authors of the foundation's Project 2025 now staff Trump's second term, where the President revived a civil-service order the plan recommended. Legal networks shape who sits on the bench: the Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, helped draw up Trump's Supreme Court shortlist, its members filled 43 of the 51 appeals-court places in his first term, and he has called it his 'recommending source' on judges.

Industry-funded groups such as ALEC go further and draft the laws themselves. Companies pay to sit with state legislators and write model bills with them, and the legislators then file the bills as their own; a 2019 investigation found at least 10,000 such copied bills in US states, more than 2,100 of which became law.

For voters, it means some decisions are talked through first with people they never elected, in private meetings, and some laws carry wording written by companies. A judge picked through one legal network can shape rulings for decades after the president who chose them has left office.
uncertain: No court or inquiry has found that these bodies directed any official's decisions; the link is drawn from who wrote the texts and who was then appointed. Trump distanced himself from Project 2025 during his 2024 campaign; the link rests on who was then appointed. The account of Leonard Leo routing money to a Supreme Court justice's wife comes from press reporting.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary:
Some movements aim to take over the state itself rather than steer it from outside. Across the Arab world the main example is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power, together with the parties that grew out of it. A smaller movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir, wants a single Islamic state, or caliphate, and has tried to get there by recruiting army officers.

In most countries the Brotherhood tradition has gone through elections. Parties from it have won seats and cabinet posts in Egypt, Jordan and Kuwait, and in Egypt and Jordan won the presidency or became the largest party in parliament. The usual sequence afterwards is that the army or the palace pushes back: the party is removed, its leaders jailed and the movement banned. The clearest case is Egypt, where the Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the presidency in 2012, the army removed him a year later and the government declared the group a terrorist organisation.

Sudan shows the other route. In 1989 Omar al-Bashir took power in a coup organised with the National Islamic Front, a movement derived from the Brotherhood, and over 30 years its supporters were placed in state jobs, including the courts, building on posts the movement had held since its leader became attorney general in 1979. Its leaders and an allied militia still hold posts and fight beside the army in the current war, and several have been sanctioned by the United States and Europe. Hizb ut-Tahrir has tried the army more directly: in 2012 a Pakistani military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to it, and in the same year Bangladesh's army linked it to a coup plot by serving officers.

For voters in these countries, it has meant seeing parties they elected win office and then be banned, with membership now punishable by prison in Egypt. In Sudan, people placed by the old regime still hold posts, and Islamist militias have a say in whether civilian rule returns. title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary:
Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet in private lodges and promise to help one another, and joining a lawful lodge is not a crime. The cases kept here are those where a lodge or secret brotherhood had its members in police forces, intelligence services, the armed forces or the courts, and those members used their posts for it. They come from Italy, Argentina, Britain and the United States, and span nearly two centuries, from a Masonic sheriff convicted in New York in 1827 over the abduction of a former member who was about to publish the lodges' rituals, to Italian court rulings in 2020.

Italy shows how far a secret lodge can go. P2, a lodge run by businessman Licio Gelli, had on its 1981 membership list the heads of all three intelligence services, the chief of defence staff, the commander of the financial police and nearly two hundred military officers. Gelli and a P2 intelligence general were convicted of planting false evidence to mislead the inquiry into the 1980 Bologna station bombing. Italy then banned secret associations that try to influence public bodies, and still prosecutes under that law, including against a senior judge. P2 reached Argentina too, where its members included the navy chief and junta member Admiral Massera, who used his position to get Gelli an adviser's post and Argentine diplomatic passports.

In the United States the brotherhood in question has sometimes been the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society. In the 1920s a Klansman mayor of Denver, under Klan pressure, made a fellow Klansman his police chief, so that the city's police became in effect a Klan body.

In Britain the claims come from inside the police. A journalist's 1984 book described Freemasons spread through British forces, with a London lodge helping secure the Metropolitan Police Commissioner's post for a chosen candidate, and a detective has said that Masonic officers took him off a corruption inquiry once it pointed to Freemasonry.

For someone in court or under investigation, the risk is that the officer or judge handling the case answers to a lodge as well as to the law. In most countries there is no rule that lets people find out whether they belong to one.

This pattern explains where today's leading foreign-policy institutes, Chatham House in London and the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) in New York, came from. Both grew out of a network of British imperialists formed around Cecil Rhodes, the mining magnate and premier of the Cape Colony, and Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa. The offices its members held are on the public record; the claim that they formed one secret society rests mainly on the historian Carroll Quigley.

The network worked by placing a small circle of like-minded men in the posts where imperial and foreign policy was made, and by giving them private clubs and journals in which to agree on that policy first. It began in South Africa, where from 1901 Milner filled the government of the conquered Boer republics with young Oxford graduates, known as Milner's Kindergarten, who went on to press for the union of the colonies in 1910. Over the next forty years men from the same circle ran the prime minister's private office, edited The Times, where one cut stories to spare German opinion during appeasement, and, as Governor-General of South Africa, refused an election and installed Smuts as prime minister. A study group of the network, joined by India Office officials, worked out the 'dyarchy' system that the government wrote into the Government of India Act 1919.

In 1919 a Kindergarten member, Lionel Curtis, convened the Paris meeting that led to Chatham House. Its American counterpart, the CFR, secretly wrote postwar planning papers for the US State Department during the Second World War, paid for by the Rockefeller Foundation, and the department classified and circulated them as its own. A CFR memo on Greenland was taken up by President Roosevelt, and the leader of its study group on occupied Germany, Allen Dulles, was recruited by the wartime spy agency to carry the plans out and later ran the CIA.

For the public, the result was that a few hundred men had regular private access to ministers and wrote papers that governments then used. Membership of these bodies was and is lawful; what voters could not see was how much of policy had been drafted in their private meetings before it reached government.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

summary:
Some of today's arrangements go back to the Cold War. Between 1945 and 1990, governments and their allies in western Europe, Turkey, Greece and Argentina, fearing communism, built secret structures inside their own states: armed networks hidden in intelligence services, officers' societies and a secret Masonic lodge. Many of them answered to people outside the elected government, and some were paid for from abroad.

NATO countries set up 'stay-behind' networks: groups of armed civilians with hidden weapons caches, meant to resist a Soviet invasion and run by military intelligence with NATO coordination and, in some countries, NATO, British or US money. Most parliaments did not know they existed until Italy's prime minister disclosed Italy's network, called Gladio, in 1990. NATO secretly funded Belgium's network inside its military intelligence and State Security services, and in Turkey a US-funded unit sat inside the army without the prime minister's knowledge. Alongside these networks, officers' societies and ultranationalist groups worked with police and ministers: in Greece members of a secret officers' society led the 1967 coup, and in Turkey the leader of the Grey Wolves, an ultranationalist movement whose gunmen later worked with police, served as deputy prime minister. In Belgium a neo-Nazi group had members in the national gendarmerie and at a NATO site.

The clearest single case is P2, a secret Masonic lodge in Italy run by Licio Gelli. Its 1981 membership list held 962 names, among them members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly two hundred military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services, and in Argentina it included junta officers, ministers, ambassadors and an interim president. Publishing the list brought down Italy's government. Foreign intelligence services also bought influence in friendly countries, as South Korea's did with members of the US Congress in the 1970s.

For people living under these arrangements, the police, army and intelligence services answered partly to networks no voter had heard of, and governments could not be held to account for what those networks did. Families of people killed in that period are still waiting on courts: in 2025 Italian judges made final a verdict that named Gelli as the knowing financier of the 1980 Bologna station bombing. Many of the ways money is hidden inside the banking system today were worked out by two banks of the 1970s and 1980s that served governments, intelligence figures and criminals: Italy's Banco Ambrosiano and BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International. Their records, spread across countries from the Americas to the Gulf and the Vatican, show the methods plainly, and the same methods are still in use.

The first method is the front owner. A bank, or the state behind it, buys other banks through people who appear to own them on their own account, so regulators never see who is in control. BCCI, mostly owned by the Abu Dhabi government and ruling family by 1991, secretly controlled First American, the largest bank in Washington, through fronts that included a former Saudi intelligence chief, while US regulators were told it was not involved; it did the same in California and Brazil.

The second is buying the officials who supervise or deposit with the bank. BCCI paid the debts of a serving US budget chief, used associates of Brazil's president as front owners, was charged with paying officials of Argentina's central bank, which regulated it, and was accused of paying Peru's central bank officials, who then deposited about three-tenths of the country's cash reserves with it.

The third is routing money through offshore companies and through institutions that national courts cannot reach. Banco Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982 with about $1.3 billion missing through offshore firms tied to the Vatican Bank, its main shareholder; Italy's top court ruled that a treaty kept the Vatican Bank's president out of reach of Italian courts. Ambrosiano's chairman belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge whose membership list of 962 names included ministers, generals and the heads of Italy's intelligence services, and the lodge's head was convicted of fraud over the money that vanished. Earlier, Michele Sindona, a banker who laundered Mafia money, had been made the Vatican's financial adviser.

For depositors and taxpayers, the losses arrived when the banks failed, and officials who banked or borrowed there had escaped checks at home. Front owners, offshore companies, banks in small jurisdictions and treaties that place some institutions outside national courts are still how hidden money moves.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

summary:
In a number of countries during the 19th and 20th centuries, a sworn society with secret or semi-secret membership decided who governed. The societies were of three kinds: ethnic or religious fraternities that filled cabinets and city halls with their members, white-supremacist and anti-immigrant orders that won elections in parts of the United States, and secret officers' societies inside armies that took power by force. Most of these arrangements ended by the 1990s, but the laws, institutions and divisions they built are still felt.

South Africa is the fullest case. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918, and by 1979 so did all but two cabinet ministers and the heads of the army and the intelligence service. Its members wrote and ran apartheid, and the list stayed hidden until journalists printed it in 1978.

The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, held office in the same way in Northern Ireland and Canada. Every prime minister of Northern Ireland from 1921 to 1969 belonged to it. For the first half of the 20th century Toronto's city hall was run by its members: every mayor in that period belonged to it, as did four Canadian prime ministers. A rival French-Canadian secret society worked to place its members in federal posts, and in Ireland a justice minister who belonged to a Catholic order reportedly gave its council private undertakings on government conduct.

In the United States in the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, won the governorships of Indiana and Colorado and put its members in charge of city police, as in Denver; seventy years earlier a secret anti-immigrant order had taken the Massachusetts government. In Serbia and Greece, secret officers' societies inside the army supplied prime ministers and led coups.

For people outside the society, this meant laws made and enforced by one closed group. Black South Africans lived under apartheid laws written by a cabinet drawn almost entirely from one secret body, and Irish Catholics in Massachusetts faced laws aimed at them. Where members filled a police force or civil service, appointments and arrests favoured them.

Across the cases on this map, from more than 80 countries and stretching from the 1890s to today, infiltration usually comes to light in one of a few ways: a seized membership list, a leak to journalists, a parliamentary or judicial inquiry, a UN panel of experts reporting on a war, an outside funder's auditors going through their own grants, another government's sanctions, or occasionally an accident that puts a wanted man and an official in the same place. Very little of it is found by the institution that was infiltrated. What follows is often a purge, and then, in a large share of cases, a partial or full reversal.

Exposure can be sudden and large. When Italian police found the membership list of P2, a secret Masonic lodge, in 1981, it named ministers, generals and the heads of all three intelligence services, and parliament dissolved the lodge and banned secret associations. Purges can be just as large, and are often carried out by decree. Governments remove judges, police officers and civil servants in their thousands, often without an individual hearing for each. Italy's government has dissolved town councils and health authorities found to be under mafia influence 402 times since 1991, many of them more than once.

Reversals follow in many countries. Courts annul convictions because evidence was gathered illegally or the wrong court heard the case, as Brazil's Supreme Court did with Lula's corruption convictions in 2021. From the 1930s to the end of the Cold War, the intelligence services of the Soviet Union and its allies in Eastern Europe placed or recruited their own people inside the governments, armies and spy agencies of Western countries. The usual method was patient: a young graduate or junior official who sympathised with communism, or who needed money, was recruited early and then left to rise. The aim was to read the other side's plans from the inside, and in some cases to nudge its policy.

The record on this map runs through Britain, the United States, West Germany, Canada, France, Belgium, Norway, Sweden, Israel and Japan, and it reaches some of the most closely guarded rooms of the period: the atomic bomb programme at Los Alamos, NATO's war plans, the US Treasury and State Department, and the counter-intelligence sections that were supposed to catch such agents. Britain's Kim Philby, recruited at Cambridge in 1934, rose to run MI6's section working against Soviet intelligence. In West Germany, East German intelligence placed Günter Guillaume as a personal aide to Chancellor Willy Brandt. Wartime Soviet cables decrypted by the US Venona programme pointed to several hundred Americans with covert Soviet ties, under half of them identified.

For the people of these countries, the result was that decisions about war, nuclear weapons and alliances were being reported to a foreign power by officials they had trusted, and that agents sent behind the Iron Curtain were betrayed by colleagues at home. Spy services and royal treasuries of powerful states have paid foreign heads of state, generals and political parties, and in some cases chosen who would rule. The method is direct: cash to a leader's office, money to one party before an election, a monthly retainer to a security chief, or support for a coup and then funding for the government that follows.

For most of the 20th century the best documented paymaster is the CIA. Released US files and court records show it funding parties before elections in Italy, Japan, Lebanon, Indonesia and British Guiana, paying King Hussein of Jordan for two decades, and keeping on its books men who ran or came to run their countries, including Panama's Manuel Noriega, Peru's spy chief Vladimiro Montesinos and two future presidents of Mexico. In Iran in 1953 it bribed members of parliament and organised the security forces to remove an elected prime minister who had nationalised the country's oil.

The same practice continues, with more paymasters. Saudi Arabia has run its Yemen policy through a committee that has paid tribal, military and political leaders since 1962; a list printed in 2012 named about 2,700 of them. A firm belonging to the UAE's security adviser is reported to have secretly bought 49% of the US president's family crypto company. Regional powers do the same next door: Pakistan's ISI in Afghanistan, Syria's intelligence in Lebanon, India's RAW in the Maldives, and Russia through party funding in Moldova.

For people in these countries, it means that the person they see in charge may owe their position, or a regular income, to another government. Policies on oil, bases, borders and who gets arrested can be decided with that paymaster in mind. Where a security chief was on a foreign payroll, as in Chile, Guatemala and Peru, the killings and disappearances carried out under him took place while he was being paid by a foreign agency.
uncertain: The US cases rest largely on declassified CIA and State Department records and are well documented, though historians debate how far US money decided outcomes rather than backing sides that were already strong. Gulf and South Asian cases depend more on leaked cables, testimony and press reports; the 2012 Yemeni payroll list was denied by the parties named, and claims about RAW in the Maldives come from press reporting.

summary:
In many countries the government of the 20th century was founded by a secret society: a sworn group that recruited inside the army or among students and exiles, kept its membership hidden, and then took power in a coup or revolution. Once in power, its members filled the cabinet, the high command and the security services, and the society often became the core of the ruling party.

Two forms recur. The first is the revolutionary society of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as the Carbonari in Naples, the Committee of Union and Progress in the Ottoman Empire, the Irish Republican Brotherhood and Siam's Khana Ratsadon, founded by students in Paris, which recruited officers and officials, used army units to force change, and then often supplied the new state's leaders. The second is the officers' lodge, a cell of mostly junior officers inside the army itself. Egypt's Free Officers seized power in 1952, and their model was copied by officers in Iraq, Libya and Sudan; similar secret groups put officers in power in Argentina, Bolivia, Syria, South Korea and Venezuela. In Spain before the 1936 coup, the clandestine Unión Militar Española was estimated to include almost half of all serving officers.

Some of these societies did not take the top office at first but worked on the state from inside the army: Japan's Sakurakai plotted two coups from inside the army's General Staff, Iraq's Golden Square colonels decided which cabinets survived before seizing power in 1941, and the RAM movement in the Philippine army helped oust Marcos in the 1980s and then tried to overthrow Aquino.

Much of today's political map still rests on this. Egypt's top military council descends from the Free Officers' command council; Syria was ruled by a member of the Ba'ath Military Committee and then his son until 2024; South Korea's army and presidency were held by members of the Hanahoe officers' club through the 1980s. For people in these countries it has meant governments formed by oath inside barracks rather than by voters, an army that sees itself as the owner of the state, and a habit of further coups by the next secret cell.
uncertain: The membership and size of secret societies are known mostly from members' memoirs and later histories, so figures such as the UME's share of officers are estimates. Historians disagree over how far some groups directed policy rather than lobbied for it. A few cases, like the 1995 Islamist officers' plot in Pakistan, failed and are included to show the method rather than its success.

title: Creditors who took over countries' finances
case_titles: Creditor powers placed commissioners over Egypt's debt payments

summary:
When a country could not pay its foreign debts, its creditors sometimes took over the part of its government that collected and spent money. Between the 1870s and the 1930s this happened across the Mediterranean, Latin America and the Caribbean: bondholders or creditor governments put their own commissioners inside the debtor state, gave them the right to collect named taxes, customs duties or state monopolies, and paid the lenders first.

The Ottoman Empire's Public Debt Administration, set up in 1881, collected a share of the empire's taxes for European bondholders. In Egypt a creditors' commission sat over the debt from 1876, and Britain's Evelyn Baring later ran the country's finances. Greece handed control of its salt, tobacco and other revenues to a six-power commission that stayed in Athens from 1898 to 1936. In Nicaragua and Haiti, New York banks took over the national bank and, with US backing, the customs and finances, in Haiti's case with US Marines removing the bank's gold to New York in 1914. After the First World War, the Dawes Plan placed creditor nominees on half of Germany's central bank board.

The same idea has returned in modern form. In Liberia after its civil war, the IMF and World Bank arranged for foreign officials to co-sign spending at the state's main revenue-earning firms.

For the people of these countries, the debt came first. Taxes on salt, tobacco and customs, which fell on ordinary households, went to foreign lenders before schools or wages, and decisions about the budget were taken by officials answerable to bondholders abroad. In several cases the arrangement lasted decades, and the resentment it caused shaped later nationalist movements in Egypt, Turkey and Haiti.
uncertain: The facts of these arrangements are well recorded in treaties and decrees. What is debated is their effect: some economic historians argue that creditor control restored credit and lowered borrowing costs, while others stress the transfer of revenue abroad and the loss of self-government. Liberia's co-signing scheme was agreed by its own transitional government, and opinions differ on whether it was imposed.

Companies and wealthy businessmen pay ministers, lawmakers, regulators and judges for contracts, licences, laws and rulings they want. Foreign firms do it to win arms, oil, aircraft and telecoms deals abroad; domestic firms do it to win public works, fishing quotas or a favourable vote at home. The payment usually travels through an agent, a consultancy, a relative or a party fund, so that it looks like a fee or a donation.

This map records such cases in about 60 countries. The largest come out of US and British foreign-bribery prosecutions: aircraft makers, arms firms, oil traders, engineering groups and telecoms companies have admitted paying officials across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Siemens, for example, paid more than $100 million to Argentine officials, including former presidents, for a national identity-card contract. At home, the same trade has brought down governments. In Italy in the early 1990s the Mani pulite inquiry found that companies' kickbacks to ruling parties were a regular part of winning public works, and at one point more than half of parliament was under indictment. In Japan, Lockheed's payments reached the office of Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka.

The pattern also reaches the officials meant to police business. Bankers and businessmen in Japan, Vietnam, Latvia, China and Antigua have paid bank inspectors and central bank chiefs, and in Slovakia businessmen's reach extended into the courts and the police leadership.

For people in these countries, the cost is paid twice. The bribe is built into the price, so hospitals, dams, weapons and ID cards cost more and are sometimes not delivered at all; and the contract or law goes to the payer rather than to the best offer or the public need. Where the payment reached the inspector or the judge, a complaint about the firm goes to someone it has already paid.

Several, including claims about Tullow Oil in Uganda and Thales in South Africa, rest on leaked documents or trials still under way. summary:
International bodies hand out things governments and companies want: the right to host the Olympics or a World Cup, UN contracts, inspection reports, standards and the direction of international courts and police bodies. Because a small number of people make these decisions, states and businesses try to get those people on their side, by paying voters, placing their own officials in top posts or using inspectors and staff to gather intelligence.

The sports bodies show it most plainly. Members of the International Olympic Committee and FIFA's executive committee are accused, and in some cases convicted, of taking money for their votes on the 2016 Rio Olympics, the 2020 Tokyo Games and the 2018 and 2022 World Cups. Police bodies have been taken over outright: in 1938 Nazi SS generals took the presidency of the international police commission that became Interpol and moved its headquarters to Berlin.

The UN has been reached from several sides. The head of its Oil-for-Food programme was accused of taking payments from Saddam Hussein's government, a UN procurement officer took bribes from contractors, and a Chinese energy firm paid a former president of the General Assembly. US intelligence used UN weapons inspectors in Iraq to spy on Saddam's government, and Russian military intelligence tried to place an officer at the International Criminal Court under a false identity. Spy services also recruit staff already inside: the CIA had a senior UN official, the Secretariat's head of political affairs, passing it Soviet secrets in the 1970s.

For people around the world, these bodies are meant to be neutral referees: deciding fairly where public money for stadiums goes, which fugitives are arrested, and whether a war crime is investigated. When their votes and posts are bought, the result is costly tournaments awarded to the highest payer, police bodies turned to one government's ends, and investigations that bend to the powerful.

title: Armed and political movements with their own people inside the state
summary:
The outside party in these cases is a movement: an armed group, a religious or nationalist movement, or a party machine. Its members end up inside the police, the army, a ministry, a court, an election office or a state-owned company, and those bodies then act in the movement's interest. Two routes recur. In one the state agrees to it, folding fighters into the army or handing a ministry to a movement's leader. In the other the movement gets its people in quietly, by recruiting serving officers or by putting members forward for posts.

The agreed route runs through governments emerging from war. Iraq's Interior Ministry, which runs the police, went in 2005 to Bayan Jabr, a former commander of the Badr Organization, a militia formed in Iran in 1982; most of its fighters had joined the new army and police, and the UN's human rights chief later said hundreds of people had been tortured or executed under the ministry. In Libya, Abdel Ghani al-Kikli's Tripoli armed group was turned into the Stability Support Apparatus and placed under the Presidential Council in 2021, and the Radaa militia held Mitiga, the capital's only airport handling commercial flights, along with prisons, as part of the state's security forces. In eastern Congo the rebel CNDP was folded into the national army and an ICC suspect served as a general. The same arrangement ran in wartime Europe: Romania's Iron Guard was given the interior ministry and the prefect's office in all fifty counties in 1940, and Germany put Hungary's Arrow Cross in power in 1944, after which its officers helped restart the deportation of Jews from Budapest.

The quiet route shows up in armies and police forces at war and at peace. The US auditor of Afghan war spending counted 31 insider attacks in the first quarter of 2021, killing 115 Afghan soldiers and police, carried out by Taliban men who had enlisted in the forces they attacked. Somalia's spy agency arrested ten al-Shabaab agents inside government bodies in 2023, and a UN panel found the group reading cargo manifests at Mogadishu port. Nigeria held 18 soldiers and 15 police in 2025 over alleged arms sales to militants. In Northern Ireland a 1973 British military intelligence report estimated that 5 to 15 per cent of Ulster Defence Regiment soldiers were or had been in loyalist paramilitary groups, and called the regiment their best single source of weapons. An Islamic Jihad cell inside Egypt's army killed President Sadat in 1981, and in the same year a bomb planted by a man working in Iran's prime minister's office killed the country's president and prime minister.

Not every movement here is armed. ThePrint counted 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Narendra Modi's second government as having come from the RSS, the Hindu nationalist organisation from whose political wing the party grew. Members of Nippon Kaigi, a lobby campaigning to rewrite Japan's constitution, held 15 of the 19 seats in Shinzo Abe's 2014 cabinet. Militant, a Trotskyist group, worked secretly inside the Labour Party, and councillors it backed took Liverpool City Council in 1983 and set an illegal budget. After Bangladesh's government fell in 2024, 30 of 47 newly appointed university vice-chancellors had ties to teachers' groups linked to the BNP or Jamaat, and the adviser overseeing education said he had asked the BNP secretary general for names. In Mesa County, Colorado, the elected clerk made false credentials for an activist of the movement claiming the 2020 election was stolen, who copied the county's voting system; she was convicted on seven counts in 2024.

For people living with this, the force they call for protection may share the aims of the group threatening them. Minorities, migrants and political opponents are affected first: a police ministry led by a movement hostile to them, an officer who belongs to a militia, an army unit that will not act against its own side. The same placements reach bodies that are not usually thought of as targets — a list of university appointments, a county election office, and Yemen's state airline, run in Sanaa by Houthi loyalists while about 100 million dollars of its money stayed under their control.
uncertain: Some of these counts come from press investigations rather than official findings. The Nippon Kaigi and RSS cabinet figures count ministers' membership and background; they are not findings that either cabinet took instructions from the movement. Claims by governments that an enemy movement has members inside the state can be political: Nigeria's president named no one, and the account of the 1981 bombing in Tehran is Iran's own. TÜGVA says the leaked lists of its candidates for army, police and judicial posts are forged. The Golden Dawn finding rests on the party's support inside the force and on at least one officer's conduct, not on proof that the police as a whole served the party.

summary:
Organised crime does not only buy officials; it also places or recruits people inside private businesses. Cocaine networks recruit staff at container ports, airports and shipping lines; laundering networks recruit bank employees; mafias and gangs take over ordinary firms so that their money passes through what looks like normal trade.

The ports of northern Europe show it most clearly. In Rotterdam and Antwerp, gangs have recruited terminal planners, IT contractors and security guards to hand over the PIN codes that release containers, so that their crews can remove the drugs before customs checks. Similar recruitment is recorded at Schiphol airport, among airport ground staff in Spain, among truck drivers in Ontario and in the crew of a container ship. In banking, laundering networks bribed staff at TD Bank in the United States to move more than $670 million, and a Credit Suisse banker handled money for a Bulgarian cocaine group.

Some groups own the business outright. Brazil's PCC, a gang born in São Paulo's prisons, is accused of running city bus companies, investment funds, a port terminal and more than a thousand petrol stations. In Italy the 'Ndrangheta has taken over firms in the north, Japanese yakuza placed workers in the state-funded Fukushima clean-up, and mafias secretly owned Malta-licensed betting companies.

For ordinary people, this puts crime money into places they use every day: the bus they ride, the petrol they buy, the bank that holds their savings. Honest firms lose contracts to companies that do not need to make a profit, workers inside ports and banks are pressured or threatened into helping, and the money that pays for violence elsewhere is cleaned through businesses that look legitimate.
uncertain: Several cases, including most of the PCC's alleged holdings, rest on prosecutors' charges that have not yet been tried. How widely insiders are recruited at ports is estimated from the cases that reach court, which are thought to be a small share.
